key_insight: Time is a learnable visual concept: by leveraging multimodal cues and the intrinsic temporal structure of videos, models can both perceive changes in playback speed and synthesize videos at different speeds.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the lack of methods for perceiving and controlling the passage of time in video: detecting whether a clip has been sped up or slowed down and generating realistic speed-altered videos.
method: Learn a 'flow of time' representation from videos using multimodal signals (visual frames, audio) and temporal structure, often via self-supervised objectives.
Train predictors to estimate time-scaling factors or classify speed changes from learned temporal embeddings.
Manipulate video playback by temporal resampling/interpolation or learned temporal warping (and align audio) to synthesize realistic faster/slower versions.
impact: Provides tools for robust temporal reasoning and controllable video editing—beneficial for action recognition, data augmentation, video synthesis, simulation, and human-centered video analysis.
visual_elements: Timeline diagram showing original video with arrows indicating sped-up and slowed-down directions (before/after frames aligned to timeline).
Model block diagram: multimodal encoder -> temporal embedding -> time-scale predictor + temporal warper/generator.
Side-by-side frame sequence examples: original vs slowed vs sped versions to show visual artifacts and fidelity.
Chart or infographic summarizing performance (e.g., speed-detection accuracy or qualitative realism) and a small t-SNE of learned temporal embeddings.
paper_title: Seeing Fast and Slow: Learning the Flow of Time in Videos
paper_authors: Yen-Siang Wu, Rundong Luo, Jingsen Zhu, Tao Tu, Ali Farhadi
